This page corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 47-3013.00 "Helpers--Electricians" (Helpers--Electricians): help electricians by performing duties requiring less skill: using, supplying, or delivering materials and tools, and cleaning the work area and equipment. Official scope text: Help electricians by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. The core tasks listed by O*NET include (that page lists 25 tasks and displays the 5 most important by default): stripping insulation from wire ends with wire strippers and connecting conductors to wiring terminals for subsequent soldering; using test instruments to troubleshoot short circuits in wiring; measuring and cutting and bending wire and conduit with measuring instruments and hand tools; checking electrical equipment for loose connections and damaged insulation and tightening connections with hand tools; and maintaining tools, vehicles, and equipment and keeping parts and supplies orderly. Common job titles include Electrical Helper and Electrician Helper and Electrician Apprentice and Electrical Apprentice and Inside Wireman Apprentice. Fit signals | The work activity importance for U.S. O*NET 47-3013.00 shows: making decisions and solving problems (88) and inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (84) and performing general physical activities (82) and processing information (81) and obtaining information (80) and handling and moving objects (80) and communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (79) are this occupation's most important activities; the work context shows: frequent face-to-face discussions (89% every day), high decision frequency (65% every day), exposure to hazardous equipment is common (51% every day), exposure to contaminants is common (55% every day), close collaboration with electricians and colleagues (56% continuous contact with others), and high precision and coordination requirements (56% extremely important). If you are willing to work hands-on around wire and conduit and electrical equipment, can do measurement and stripping and wiring and inspection solidly according to the electrician's instructions and drawings, and take responsibility for work safety and process quality and site order, this occupation's daily requirements are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (47-3013.00, work context and task scope): exposure to hazardous equipment is common (51% every day); exposure to contaminants is common (55% every day); often working in narrow or elevated spaces and in ceilings and pipe shafts; relatively serious consequences of error (17% extremely serious and 22% very serious); relatively high responsibility for others' health and safety (37% extremely high responsibility and 20% high responsibility); and time pressure from process interfaces and schedules (19% every day and 52% once a week or more). This occupation deals with wire and conduit and distribution and electrical equipment and power supply status: one instance of working without de-energizing or verifying voltage, one inadequate wiring or terminal tightening, one measurement or cutting mistake, or one inadequate protection when working at height or in ceilings can all cause electric shock, short circuits, fire, equipment damage, and schedule and compliance risk. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation needed to some preparation needed) (below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0)); the education section on that page shows 71% requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, 13% requiring a post-secondary certificate, and 11% below a high school diploma (the page does not account for the remaining 5%); growth is labeled Little or no change (0%), and that page is not marked Bright Outlook. If you find it hard to work amid dust and contaminants and noise and elevated and narrow conditions, find it hard to accept a rhythm that changes with the project and processes and outage windows and possible overtime, or are unwilling to take responsibility for safety and process coordination, you should treat these as real costs.

Taking on judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things at the same time on one task: do the technical work solidly (complete measurement and stripping and wiring and inspection and cleaning according to drawings and the electrician's instructions and procedures, producing usable material and work records), keep safety and compliance and boundaries under control (work and keep records according to de-energization and voltage verification and isolation and lockout-tagout and height and edge and machinery and cutting and occupational health requirements, distinguish publicly shareable information from controlled materials involving the project and the power supplier and manufacturers and handle them according to policy, and do not perform live work or handle out of bounds without authorization), and take on definable job responsibility (be responsible for your own measurement and stripping and wiring and fastening and inspection and records, and refer matters beyond job authorization or involving special operations and live work and major safety matters to the appropriate position or organization according to policy). It is suggested to test this with one verifiable experience (completing an assisted work plan and an explanation of material and work records for a fictitious task sheet, or a review of handling a live or short circuit or cutting anomaly), rather than relying only on the conclusion of an interest questionnaire.

Preface | The following comparison is presented in four columns: "career direction — core work and outputs — key differences — what it suits better". Electrical and carpentry and piping and painting and roofing positions often connect within the same project and process, but connection does not mean they are interchangeable; each position differs in subject matter, materials, qualifications, and responsibility boundaries and must be checked separately.

Key difference: this occupation takes wire and conduit and distribution and electrical equipment and on-site coordination as its subject matter, completing measuring and stripping and wiring and inspection and cleaning within the scope of the electrician and job authorization based on electrical coordination and tool and site ability, and is responsible for work safety and process quality and site order; adjacent positions take independent electrical installation or carpentry or piping or painting or roofing as their subject matter, with different specialties and authorization.

Better suited to people who are willing to work hands-on around wire and tools and the site, can do measuring and stripping and wiring and inspection solidly according to the electrician and drawings and procedures, and take responsibility for work safety and process quality.

Core work and outputs: selecting tools and materials from storage and delivering them to the site, measuring and cutting and bending wire and conduit, stripping insulation from wire ends and connecting them to terminals, checking for loose connections and damaged insulation and tightening, using test instruments to troubleshoot short circuits, and maintaining tools and vehicles and equipment; the outputs are assisted work completed according to drawings and procedures together with material and work records.

Responsibility preface | Efficiency can be outsourced to equipment and systems, but on-site measuring and stripping and wiring and inspection and energization judgments and safety and process responsibility cannot. The following five steps are the human responsibility points that must be preserved before and after adopting any digital tool or automated data and report generation.

Task and boundaries: the project location and circuit and electrical safety boundaries must be determined by the electrician and personnel holding the corresponding qualifications and authorization, and equipment and systems do not replace on-site and electrical judgment.

Data and methods: usage and test and material and progress data and their sources and calibration must be checked and reviewed by the person, and insufficient or deviating data must be clearly stated, and gaps must not be concealed by system output.

Conclusions and determinations: measuring and wiring and inspection and testing and restoration conclusions must be made by the person according to drawings and procedures and current standards, and system output must not be used directly as a basis for energization or rework or external publication.

Safety and compliance: de-energization and voltage verification and isolation and lockout-tagout and live work and height and edges and machinery and cutting and occupational health and work permits and personal protection must follow work safety and special operations requirements and be carried out according to policy, and controlled materials must be managed under confidentiality and retention period requirements.

Changes and disclosure: materials and circuits and wiring and process information disclosure and design or circuit changes must be carried out within the scope of authorization and policy, and when a live or short circuit or machinery or exceeding-authorization anomaly is found, operations must be paused and isolated and reported according to policy.

subject.summary: Helpers--Electricians corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 47-3013.00 "Helpers--Electricians": help electricians by performing duties requiring less skill: using, supplying, or delivering materials and tools, and cleaning the work area and equipment. Core tasks include stripping insulation from wire ends with wire strippers and connecting conductors to terminals for subsequent soldering, using test instruments to troubleshoot short circuits in wiring, measuring and cutting and bending wire and conduit with measuring instruments and hand tools, checking electrical equipment for loose connections and damaged insulation and tightening connections with hand tools, and maintaining tools and vehicles and equipment and keeping parts and supplies orderly; common job titles include Electrical Helper and Electrician Helper and Electrician Apprentice and Electrical Apprentice. Official scope text: Help electricians by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. Scope note: the U.S. wage and employment and industry data presented by O*NET on the 47-3013.00 page are not marked as taken from a parent or adjacent occupation, and this page labels them faithfully according to this occupation's (47-3013.00) own scope; this occupation is Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation needed to some preparation needed) (below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0)), with 2024—2034 growth of Little or no change (0%).
